notes: The manual doesn't give a wiring diagram for the buttons. It says to use any GPIO pins, so I used the pins from the code listing: GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO10.
gpiozero Button pins are pulled up internally. Each button therefore connects its GPIO pin to ground, with no external resistor.

Each tactile switch straddles the breadboard centre gap. Side 1 (1.l, 1.r) is in the top half and side 2 (2.l, 2.r) is in the bottom half. The GPIO lead goes into the top half of the button's column. A pin-to-pin lead runs from the bottom half to the bottom negative rail, 'bn'. The rail is a single strip, so the hole numbers are arbitrary.
The five pin-to-socket leads are jumper-wire-mf. Port a is the socket end on the Pi header and port b is the pin end in the breadboard. Four carry GPIO signals and one carries GND to the rail.
The four pin-to-pin leads were matched to the Grove cable in the parts list, which is wrong. I used the catalogue jumper-wire instead.
The tactile switches were listed as not in the catalogue, but the catalogue's pushbutton fits, so I used it.
The Raspberry Pi isn't in the catalogue, so I created a raspberry-pi type with only the header pins used here, plus an AUDIO jack port.

The speakers or headphones plug into the Pi's 3.5mm audio jack. The catalogue match was speakers-usb-powered, so I connected only its AUDIO_IN. USB_5V is left unconnected because the manual says nothing about powering the speakers.
The software steps (pygame sounds, gpiozero code, dictionary refactor) don't add physical parts.
